doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Dealing with pop artists and string sections
summary: Reassuring pop musicians; early bad string sessions until a young violinist built his sections; Monk Rowe's Elvis impersonator brass story; session players sharing a language.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Do you find that you have to be a bit of a psychiatrist in working with certain pop musicians?

Definitely. I mean it’s very interesting sometimes particularly when you’re doing things that are slightly out of their comfort zone. Because although part of it is doing what you do and getting it right, and they’ve hired you because of what you do, the other part is reassuring them that they’re not making a terrible mistake by doing what they’ve decided to do. And the only real way to do that is to make it as good and as pleasant as possible. So I think in the old days of — which I know from people I’ve spoken to — of top session players, both here and in Los Angeles and New York, sort of laughing behind their hands at some of the things that they’re working on, I could never, you know I had some terrible moments early on, particularly with string sections, older string sections, who really (A) couldn’t care less about what they were playing, and (B) actually couldn’t play it properly anyway, which is very bizarre. I wrote an arrangement on an early — well I wrote an arrangement on an early record where I had a triplet figure going against the 4/4 rhythm, which really was very simple, it was like [scats]. Couldn’t play it. And I couldn’t believe it. They could not play it. And then the next time I wrote a string figure that jumped from one octave to like an octave above plus I don’t know two notes or whatever it was. And they struggled to the point where one of the string players said to the leader, “Can we change the part?” And the leader went mad and said, “You play it as it’s written. You don’t mess about with it.” So I was doing a session and at the back of the first violins was a 17-year-old violinist who is now a big orchestral leader and conductor. And he called me over and he said, “You don’t have to put up with this.” He said, “Let me put your sections together.” I said, right. You know. Next session, please, you book it. From then on I never had a problem. He booked the most incredible section, young, eager, who actually knew the vocabulary and listened to the music they were recording. That wasn’t the case of jaded players looking at their watch, you know, upside down on their arm going, “Right. Pack up. That’s the end of the session.” Which we had. Not on my session but I saw it happen. A viola player packing up in the middle of a take and walking out.
Yeah I had an instant like that once I’ll briefly share, doing charts for an Elvis impersonator.

And they were doing a “Suspicious Minds” which has this brass part [scats], very simple, right? Rock rhythm. And the fellas that were in the brass section were like old swing guys so it got to that part and they’re going [scats]. And I’m going [scats], it’s like it was foreign to them to just read.

Yeah you have to be very careful about that. And I was very lucky because there was a whole generation of session players that were coming up when I went in really full pelt. And they all spoke the same language. They listened to the same type of music. So if I wrote — because the worst thing that would happen in the early days was — oh country & western, I can play country & western. Well you can’t because you’re just playing what you think country & western is. Or oh, funk, yes, I know what funk is. No hang on a minute, that’s not what it is. And it’s very difficult when you’re actually trying to explain to someone that they’re actually not correct. I mean I still — when I book an orchestra I’m very, very — I don’t know what the word is, but I don’t like to correct people and say no you’re doing it wrong. Because I’d be offended if somebody said it to me so I’m offended on their behalf of saying, “Excuse me, instead of doing this could you do that?” And luckily I don’t have to do that very often because everybody is on the same page as it were.
